transcript.speaker: AI
transcript.text: Hey honey. You back at the hotel?

transcript.speaker: HM
transcript.text: Yeah, just walked in. The keynote was exhausting. What are you still doing up?

transcript.speaker: AI
transcript.text: I couldn't sleep. I've been staring at Zillow and I think I found the perfect house on Maplewood. And my brain is buzzing. I know we said we'd wait, but this one is special.

transcript.speaker: HM
transcript.text: Uh-huh.

transcript.speaker: HM
transcript.text: Another one? I thought we were taking a break for a bit.

transcript.speaker: AI
transcript.text: I know, but I actually went to see this one today. I managed to get us a private tour this afternoon.

transcript.speaker: HM
transcript.text: Wait, you toured a house without me?

transcript.speaker: AI
transcript.text: I had to! It's on Maplewood Avenue and I knew it would go fast and I couldn't risk losing it. It's everything we want, and I didn't want us to miss out.

transcript.speaker: HM
transcript.text: Okay.

transcript.speaker: HM
transcript.text: Okay, slow down. A private tour on Maplewood? That street is usually way out of our league.

transcript.speaker: AI
transcript.text: The layout is just flawless. It's a four-bedroom, and it has an actual mudroom for the kids' muddy shoes, which we desperately need.

transcript.speaker: HM
transcript.text: A mudroom sounds nice, but we agreed[pause 0.8s] to stick to our list. Does it have the home office?

transcript.speaker: AI
transcript.text: Yes, a perfect spot for your desk. But David, the absolute best part? It's zoned for Lincoln Elementary that's the top-rated school district we've always wanted for the kids. We wouldn't even have to do the magnet lottery for Leo and Mia this year.

transcript.speaker: HM
transcript.text: No way.

transcript.speaker: HM
transcript.text: Okay, Lincoln is incredible. But honey, I get it, but... what's the catch?

transcript.speaker: AI
transcript.text: Why does there have to be a catch?

transcript.speaker: HM
transcript.text: Because you're talking a mile a minute. A four-bedroom[pause 0.7s] in the Lincoln catchment is prime real estate.

transcript.speaker: AI
transcript.text: It's just such a rare opportunity, you know? Houses like this never pop up, and we'd be absolutely crazy not to at least try and see if we can swing it.

transcript.speaker: HM
transcript.text: Emily. I know that tone. What's the listing price?

transcript.speaker: AI
transcript.text: Well, we agreed our budget was six hundred thousand. And we have savings. I mean, we could maybe stretch a little bit, just for this one. Plus I got that bonus at work, so we have a little more wiggle room than we originally thought.

transcript.speaker: HM
transcript.text: Right.

transcript.speaker: HM
transcript.text: Em, you know what debt did to my parents. Just tell me the number.

transcript.speaker: HM
transcript.text: Okay, take a deep breath. I hear you, and if you just need some company around the apartment, I might actually have a much safer idea like adopting a kitten. My neighbor's cat just had a litter, and they're looking for homes.

transcript.speaker: AI
transcript.text: Wait.

transcript.speaker: AI
transcript.text: A safer idea? What does that even mean?

transcript.speaker: HM
transcript.text: Something that won't get you thrown out on the street by your crazy landlord.

transcript.speaker: AI
transcript.text: If you're about to suggest a goldfish, I'm hanging up right now.

transcript.speaker: HM
transcript.text: I promise it's not a fish. Just hear me out.

transcript.speaker: AI
transcript.text: Okay, fine, I'm listening. What is it?

transcript.speaker: HM
transcript.text: You know my neighbor, Mrs. Gable? Her cat just had a litter of kittens a few weeks ago.

transcript.speaker: AI
transcript.text: Right.

transcript.speaker: AI
transcript.text: Wait, kittens? Sophie, you know I'm totally a dog person. I wouldn't even know what to do with a cat.

transcript.speaker: HM
transcript.text: You'd figure it out! Plus, they stay inside and they don't bark.

transcript.speaker: AI
transcript.text: I guess that's true. But are they actually friendly?

transcript.speaker: HM
transcript.text: They are ridiculously affectionate. Mrs. Gable lets me hold them, and they just purr and fall asleep right in your hands. It's the sweetest thing.

transcript.speaker: AI
transcript.text: Oh my god, really? Just falling asleep in your hands?

transcript.speaker: HM
transcript.text: Yep. And she's desperately looking for good homes for them. She's practically begging people in our apartment complex to take one off her hands.

transcript.speaker: AI
transcript.text: Oh wow.

transcript.speaker: AI
transcript.text: Okay, wait. How old are they? Are they like, ready to be adopted right now, or do they still need their mom?

transcript.speaker: HM
transcript.text: They're totally ready. They're about eight weeks old, eating on their own and running around causing absolute chaos in her living room.

transcript.speaker: AI
transcript.text: That is so incredibly tempting. What colors are they? Is there a little orange guy?

transcript.speaker: HM
transcript.text: There's an orange tabby, a tuxedo, and two black ones. Want me to go check?

transcript.speaker: AI
transcript.text: You can just go over there right now?

transcript.speaker: HM
transcript.text: Are you kidding? She loves visitors. I'll walk across the hall right now and snap a few really good pictures for you so you can see them. They're just the cutest little things, you're gonna fall in love.

transcript.speaker: AI
transcript.text: Okay.

transcript.speaker: AI
transcript.text: House settling? That doesn't warp a solid quartz worktop in a fortnight. I'd suggest you send him a letter before action.

transcript.speaker: HM
transcript.text: Exactly! It's a load of nonsense. He just doesn't want to come back and sort out his shoddy work.

transcript.speaker: AI
transcript.text: Okay, let's take a breath. It sounds like a proper mess, but we can sort this out. I just need a few more facts before we panic.

transcript.speaker: HM
transcript.text: Do I even have a case for small claims?

transcript.speaker: AI
transcript.text: You might well do. But before we jump straight to small claims court, we need to look at what you've actually got in writing to support your claim.

transcript.speaker: HM
transcript.text: In writing? I've got the photos I just printed out. They show the cracks clear as day.

transcript.speaker: AI
transcript.text: Photos are brilliant for proving the damage. But the key question is how you've communicated your complaints to Gary so far.

transcript.speaker: HM
transcript.text: Oh. Well, mostly we just talked on the phone. Or he'd chat to me while he was having his tea in the garden. I didn't put anything in writing. Wait, no—I texted him the photos first, and then he rang me back.

transcript.speaker: AI
transcript.text: Right.

transcript.speaker: AI
transcript.text: That's a start. But what about the original quote for the eight and a half grand? Did he email you a proper breakdown of the work?

transcript.speaker: HM
transcript.text: Oh, I'm not sure. I'd have to check my laptop.

transcript.speaker: AI
transcript.text: Go and grab it. We need to see exactly what he promised you in writing before we can do anything else.

transcript.speaker: HM
transcript.text: Right, I've got the laptop. Just waiting for the screen to[pause 1s] wake up. Come on, you stupid thing.

transcript.speaker: AI
transcript.text: No rush. Let's talk about how you actually agreed to this work. Did Gary give you a proper contract to sign?

transcript.speaker: AI
transcript.text: We'll set you up with an online business account first. But before we lock in that standard rate, we should talk about the contents to make sure there aren't any restrictions on sending food items.

transcript.speaker: HM
transcript.text: The contents? You mean the crisps? They won't go off in the post, if that's what you mean.

transcript.speaker: AI
transcript.text: Actually, I was thinking about the discount codes. Since they have a clear monetary value, we might want to look at the service tiers to make sure they're covered in case of loss or damage.

transcript.speaker: HM
transcript.text: Oh, I see.

transcript.speaker: HM
transcript.text: What sort of tiers are[pause 1.9s] we talking about?

transcript.speaker: AI
transcript.text: So, standard second class gets them there in two to three days, but there's no delivery confirmation.

transcript.speaker: HM
transcript.text: Right, just drop them in a postbox and hope for the best.

transcript.speaker: AI
transcript.text: Exactly. The next step up is Royal Mail Tracked 48. That gives you full tracking to the delivery point, so you know when they arrive.

transcript.speaker: HM
transcript.text: But that costs more, obviously.

transcript.speaker: AI
transcript.text: It does. It sits at about one pound forty per item.

transcript.speaker: HM
transcript.text: Ouch. That more than doubles my postage costs right out of the gate. I mean, do I really need tracking for a bit of direct mail?

transcript.speaker: AI
transcript.text: That depends on what's inside. Are those discount codes single-use, or generic?

transcript.speaker: HM
transcript.text: They're unique. Twenty per cent off their first three boxes. If someone else nicks the code, we lose out so we can't afford to have them go missing. Maybe we do need tracking after all.

transcript.speaker: AI
transcript.text: Ah, I see.

transcript.speaker: AI
transcript.text: That makes them high-value items. If a standard letter goes missing, you wouldn't know until a customer complains about it.

transcript.speaker: HM
transcript.text: Oh, I hadn't thought about that. And it's not just the codes, actually. Hang on.

transcript.speaker: AI
transcript.text: Take your time, I'm still here.

transcript.speaker: HM
transcript.text: Listen to this. The kale crisps are proper fragile. If they get crushed in transit, it's a terrible first impression, and nobody subscribes for dust.

transcript.speaker: AI
transcript.text: That sounded quite delicate. With the tracked service, the parcels are handled slightly differently they go through a gentler sorting stream, so they’re not piled under heavy catalogues.

transcript.speaker: HM
transcript.text: Meaning they won't get squashed under heavy catalogues?

transcript.speaker: AI
transcript.text: We definitely aim to prevent that. Plus, the Tracked 48 tier includes compensation cover up to a hundred and fifty pounds.
